uiContracts.minimumTouchTarget: var(--target) — 44x44. Write the token, not the pixel value: a literal is what no-hardcoded-design-values forbids, and it cannot be re-pointed by data-platform="mobile". var(--target-lg) is 56px, for the one action a thumb reaches for without looking.
uiContracts.minimumTouchTargetDense: var(--target-min) — 24x24, WCAG 2.2 AA SC 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum. The floor a deliberately compact control is measured against instead of var(--target), not a size it is exempted to: a dense affordance below 24x24 is a violation under touch-target-dense. 44x44 is AAA (SC 2.5.5) and this system's stricter default, which is what makes the second floor a relaxation to the standard rather than a discount off it. There is no third tier below this one and no per-element opt-out — 24x24 is the standard's own floor, so there is nothing left to be held to underneath it.

verifiedBy.minimumTouchTargetDense: @elirobinson/ai-patterns/testing/playwright → checkTouchTargets(), which measures anything matching DENSE_AFFORDANCE_SELECTOR against MINIMUM_TOUCH_TARGET_DENSE and reports a miss as touch-target-dense

vendoredElementTargets.policy: Every interactive control in @elirobinson/ai-elements, measured in a browser against the shipped tokens and classified against one of the two touch-target floors above. Elements is vendored from vercel/ai-elements and was not built to these contracts; shadcn/Radix defaults land at 32-40px, which clears WCAG 2.2 AA (SC 2.5.8) and misses this system’s 44x44 default. Each entry below reads "<verdict> — <control>. Measured <geometry>. <why it is that verdict and not the other>". The default is the primary floor: a vendored button is held to var(--target) unless it appears here as dense, so a control that nobody classified is measured strictly rather than quietly excused.
vendoredElementTargets.react-flow-attribution: exception — .react-flow__attribution a, painted by @xyflow/react into the corner of canvas, connection, controls, edge, node and toolbar. Measured 51x13. The one control this package does not fix: it is React Flow’s own licence notice, appears in no vendored class string so the transform layer cannot reach it, and React Flow’s licence requires it to stay unless a consumer holds a Pro subscription. A page that renders an Elements canvas narrows checkTouchTargets’ selector at the call site, where the exception is visible in the test — see packages/ai-elements/a11y.
vendoredElementTargets.button-floor: primary — ui/button.tsx — every <Button> in the tree. Measured default 36px, sm 32px, icon 36x36, icon-sm 32x32, icon-lg 40x40. The floor every vendored button gets unless it is classified dense elsewhere in this list. shadcn sizes at 32-40px, which clears AA and misses this system’s AAA default; the `not-data-[touch-target=dense]` guard is what keeps that a default rather than a blanket, and it cannot be undone by a consumer’s className the way a merged utility could.
vendoredElementTargets.command-item-floor: primary — ui/command.tsx — CommandItem (model, voice and mic pickers). Measured 32px tall. Choosing a model or a microphone is the whole point of the surface it sits on.
vendoredElementTargets.dropdown-item-floor: primary — ui/dropdown-menu.tsx — DropdownMenuItem (open-in-chat, prompt input action menu). Measured 32px tall. A menu row is a nav item, which contracts.json already names as primary.
vendoredElementTargets.select-item-floor: primary — ui/select.tsx — SelectItem. Measured 32px tall (PREDICTED — no fixture in the harness opens a Select menu; the markup is the same as CommandItem and DropdownMenuItem, both of which were measured). Same control, same reason. Left at a different height from the menu rows beside it, it would read as a bug.
vendoredElementTargets.tabs-trigger-floor: primary — ui/tabs.tsx — TabsTrigger (sandbox). Measured 58x38 and 64x38. [role="tab"] is in PRIMARY_CONTROL_SELECTOR by name, and a tab bar is navigation.
vendoredElementTargets.accordion-trigger-floor: primary — ui/accordion.tsx — AccordionTrigger (agent tools). Measured 1212x36 — full width, 36 tall. A disclosure row already spans its container, so height is the only axis in question and there is no density cost to answering it.
vendoredElementTargets.dialog-close-hit-area: primary — ui/dialog.tsx — the built-in close button (model selector, voice selector). Measured 16x16. The painted glyph stays 16px and the hit area grows around it, which is what contracts.json asks for — the button has no fill at rest, so nothing visible changes. 16x16 misses 24x24 as well, so declaring it dense was never available.
vendoredElementTargets.switch-hit-area: primary — ui/switch.tsx — Switch (environment variables). Measured 32x18. tokens.css floors our own switches to var(--target) on a phone, so a vendored one is not a different kind of control. A `::before` centred on the track gives the finger 44x44 while the switch stays 32x18 — the bounded overlay contracts.json prescribes. Verified against hit-area-no-overlap: the overlay reaches 22px from the track’s centre and no sibling’s centre is inside that.
vendoredElementTargets.sources-trigger-floor: primary — sources.tsx — SourcesTrigger. Measured 110x16. A 16px-tall disclosure row misses the dense floor too, so there is no second tier to fall back to.
vendoredElementTargets.source-link-floor: primary — sources.tsx — Source (the citation link). Measured 152x16. A citation marker: an a[href] that navigates away from the page, sitting in a list where every row is free to be taller.
vendoredElementTargets.reasoning-trigger-floor: primary — reasoning.tsx — ReasoningTrigger. Measured 1248x20. Same shape as SourcesTrigger: a full-width row at 20px.
vendoredElementTargets.chain-of-thought-header-floor: primary — chain-of-thought.tsx — ChainOfThoughtHeader. Measured 1248x20. Same shape again.
vendoredElementTargets.queue-section-trigger-floor: primary — queue.tsx — QueueSectionTrigger. Measured 1222x36. A full-width section header that collapses its list.
vendoredElementTargets.file-tree-row-floor: primary — file-tree.tsx — the folder/file name row. Measured 1194x20. The row is what a user aims at to open a folder; it spans the tree already.
vendoredElementTargets.file-tree-chevron-hit-area: dense — file-tree.tsx — the expand/collapse chevron beside the row. Measured 16x16. A second, redundant way to do what the row beside it already does, drawn at the size of its glyph. Dense — but 16x16 misses the dense floor as well, so it is grown to var(--target-min) rather than merely declared.
vendoredElementTargets.inline-citation-carousel-paging-floor: primary — inline-citation.tsx — InlineCitationCarouselPrev and …Next. Measured 16x16 each. Carousel paging is pagination, which contracts.json names as primary in the same breath as buttons and nav items.
vendoredElementTargets.canvas-controls-floor: primary — controls.tsx — the React Flow zoom/fit/lock cluster. Measured 26x26 each. Viewport controls on a canvas are hit repeatedly and by feel. The buttons are React Flow’s, but Elements already restyles them through `[&>button]`, so the floor goes the same way.
vendoredElementTargets.audio-player-control-bar-floor: primary — audio-player.tsx — the mute button, time display and time range in the control bar. Measured 49x32 (mute) and 63x32 (time display). A media transport is the reason the player exists, and a play button is the canonical 44px target. The play/seek buttons are <Button asChild> and are already floored by button-floor; these three are ButtonGroupText and are not, so the bar floors its own children.
vendoredElementTargets.message-action-dense: dense — message.tsx — MessageAction (copy, regenerate, rate). Measured 32x32, clears 24x24. The clearest case in this file: the message is the subject, the action is an affordance attached to it, and the row of them reads as one cluster at a single scale.
vendoredElementTargets.artifact-close-dense: dense — artifact.tsx — ArtifactClose. Measured 32x32, clears 24x24. It dismisses the artifact, which reads primary in isolation — but it is the third button in a cluster of three identical icon buttons in the same header bar, and splitting that cluster so one is 44 and two are 32 is not a density decision anybody would draw on purpose. The cluster is the unit, and the cluster is dense. Recorded here rather than left implicit because it is the closest call in this file.
vendoredElementTargets.artifact-action-dense: dense — artifact.tsx — ArtifactAction. Measured 32x32, clears 24x24. Acts on the artifact’s content — copy it, regenerate it. Same cluster as ArtifactClose.
vendoredElementTargets.code-block-copy-dense: dense — code-block.tsx — CodeBlockCopyButton. Measured 36x36, clears 24x24. Acts on the code block it sits on; the code is the subject.
vendoredElementTargets.commit-copy-dense: dense — commit.tsx — CommitCopyButton. Measured 28x28, clears 24x24. Copies the hash sitting next to it.
vendoredElementTargets.terminal-copy-dense: dense — terminal.tsx — TerminalCopyButton. Measured 28x28, clears 24x24. Copies the scrollback.
vendoredElementTargets.stack-trace-copy-dense: dense — stack-trace.tsx — StackTraceCopyButton. Measured 28x28, clears 24x24. Copies the trace.
vendoredElementTargets.suggestion-dense: dense — suggestion.tsx — Suggestion. Measured 32px tall, clears 24x24. A 32px rounded-full pill is MUI’s Chip exactly, and contracts.json already settled that a chip which is a control is dense at that scale (#114). Applying a different answer to the same shape here would be the inconsistency, not the exemption.
vendoredElementTargets.prompt-input-tool-button-dense: dense — prompt-input.tsx — PromptInputButton (the composer’s inline tool row). Measured 32x32 icon-only and 88x32 labelled, both clear 24x24. The one place in this file where two controls in the same row get different answers, and deliberately: PromptInputSubmit is the surface’s primary action and is floored to 44 by button-floor, while the tool row beside it — add an attachment, toggle search — is a strip of compact affordances at shadcn’s InputGroupButton scale. Flooring the strip too would make the whole composer footer 44px tall and remove the size difference that says which one sends the message.
vendoredElementTargets.transcription-segment-dense: dense — transcription.tsx — TranscriptionSegment. Measured 23px tall, 24x24 effective — clears 24x24. An inline target inside flowing text: clicking a word seeks the audio. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 exempts targets in a sentence outright, and this system’s own visual suite already records that an inline link in body copy is not what the 44px rule is about. The dense floor is therefore stricter than the standard here, and it still passes.

no-barrel-imports.summary: Import via package subpaths only — @elirobinson/react/components/<tier>/<Name>, @elirobinson/react/hooks/<name>, @elirobinson/tokens/tokens.css. There are no barrel files; a bare @elirobinson/react import does not resolve.
no-barrel-imports.check: Every import from an @elirobinson package names a subpath (components/*, hooks/*, styles/*.css, styles.css, tokens.css, tailwind.css, tokens.json, tokens-data, manifest, patterns, contracts, agents/*, testing/*).
no-barrel-imports.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/eslint-config → no-restricted-imports. Run `ds props <Name>` for the exact specifier.

no-foreign-component-libraries.summary: @elirobinson/react is the component vocabulary. A second library (MUI, Chakra, Ant Design, Mantine, HeroUI, Headless UI, DaisyUI) forks the system's behaviour and accessibility guarantees. Radix is already wrapped by the system, so importing it directly does the same.
no-foreign-component-libraries.check: No import resolves to a foreign component library, and no direct Radix import appears outside a repo's sanctioned gap-filler directory.

no-hardcoded-design-values.summary: Colour, radius, shadow and motion come from tokens — a mapped Tailwind utility, a .t-* class, or var(--token) in an arbitrary value. A literal cannot be re-pointed, so it silently stops responding to [data-theme="dark"] and to any token change.
no-hardcoded-design-values.check: No hex / rgb() / hsl() / oklch() literal, and no magic px or ms for radius, shadow or duration, appears in a className string, a style object, or a stylesheet that consumes values.

no-underlined-control-label.summary: A control does not underline its own label. An underline is the one visual signal a hyperlink owns; drawn under a button, chip, tab or pagination item it stops telling a reader whether the thing navigates or acts, and on a filled surface it reads as a link wearing a button. Emphasis on a control comes from the fill, the label weight, or a border. A link-styled button on no fill is a different, legitimate pattern and is out of scope.
no-underlined-control-label.check: No rule that paints a control's own filled surface also declares text-decoration: underline (or its longhand) on that control.
no-underlined-control-label.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/eslint-config/css → @elirobinson-css/no-underlined-control-label, for a consumer's own stylesheets. Inside @elirobinson/react the same property is pinned twice: component-css.test.mjs sweeps every component stylesheet for an underline, and control-affordance.test.mjs resolves the real cascade over tokens.css + the component sheets and asserts the winning declaration is not one.

control-edge-contrast.summary: A control's edge comes from --border-control, not --border or --border-strong. The decorative pair measures 1.24:1 and 1.53:1 against --bg and is for surface seams — card edges, table rules, dividers, the edge of a floating panel — where nothing depends on seeing the line. --border-control is 3.64:1 light and 3.95:1 dark in the default palette, clearing the 3:1 SC 1.4.11 asks of the boundary that tells a user where an input, switch, chip, slider, stepper or segmented control is. Both tokens measure correctly on their own, so a per-token contrast sweep cannot see the mistake; it is a component reaching for the wrong one.
control-edge-contrast.check: No rule whose selector names a control paints a border (border, border-color, or any side/logical longhand) with var(--border) or var(--border-strong). The test: if the border were invisible, would the user lose the control?
control-edge-contrast.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/eslint-config/css → @elirobinson-css/no-decorative-control-edge, for a consumer's own stylesheets. Inside the system the same property is pinned twice: component-css.test.mjs sweeps every component stylesheet for a decorative token on a control edge, and packages/tokens' contrast.test.mjs re-measures --border-control against every neutral surface in every palette x theme combination — which is the authority for the ratios quoted above, so re-tuning any palette fails there rather than leaving this summary quietly wrong.

status-surface-foreground.summary: A status surface is three tokens that only work together. --status-success | warning | danger | info is the fill and is never text; --status-X-on is the text drawn on that fill; --status-X-fg is status-coloured text on --bg or --surface; --status-X-tint with --status-X-tint-edge is the quiet pair. --status-success and --status-warning stopped being brand aliases and now own palette-independent hues, so a foreground that flips with the theme — var(--fg-inverse), or the legacy var(--fg-on-signal) — no longer tracks the fill it sits on and misses 4.5:1 in whichever theme it was not measured in. --status-warning is 1.87:1 against --bg in light, a documented SC 1.4.11 exception that holds only while the hue is a fill and the text on it carries the contrast; as a line it is the whole signal, so a warning fill or rule is edged with --status-warning-border (3.76:1 light, 11.22:1 dark). --fg-on-signal survives only as an alias of --accent-fg and collapses under any non-default palette.
status-surface-foreground.check: No rule that paints a status fill (background or background-color set to var(--status-success | warning | danger | info)) also sets color to var(--fg-inverse) or var(--fg-on-signal) — the text on a status fill is var(--status-<state>-on). No border, outline or column-rule colour is var(--status-warning) — an edge is var(--status-warning-border). No value anywhere, including a custom-property definition, references var(--fg-on-signal). The -on, -fg, -tint, -tint-edge and -border members are the fixes and are never the defect.
status-surface-foreground.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/eslint-config/css → @elirobinson-css/no-mismatched-status-foreground, for a consumer's own stylesheets. Inside the system the same property is pinned by packages/tokens' contrast.test.mjs, which sweeps palette x theme and asserts every --status-X-on against its own fill in all four combinations, and asserts the --status-warning exception from both sides — the fill under 3:1 against --bg and --status-warning-border over it.

forward-ref.summary: Every component that renders a focusable or interactive native element uses forwardRef, forwarding to the outermost interactive element the component owns.
forward-ref.check: The component is wrapped in React.forwardRef and the forwarded ref resolves to the interactive DOM node (or a documented handle, e.g. VirtualListHandle).
forward-ref.verifiedBy: not automated — review. Applies to contributions to @elirobinson/react itself.

touch-target-primary.summary: Primary interactive controls at their default size — buttons, pagination items, segmented-control options, nav items — have a minimum touch target of var(--target) square (44x44px, and what every primary control gets under data-platform="mobile" and on a coarse-pointer phone; the dense tier is excluded from that floor by name rather than inflated to it, because it is already measured against 24x24). Reach for the token, not the number: a literal is what no-hardcoded-design-values forbids, and it cannot be re-pointed by the platform dial. Where visual density matters, keep the painted glyph small and expand the hit area with padding or a bounded overlay rather than inflating the visible control. A control whose whole purpose is to be compact belongs under touch-target-dense instead; padding it back up to var(--target) only turns it into the default size and removes the reason the compact variant exists.
touch-target-primary.check: The computed hit area of each primary control is at least var(--target) square, measured on whichever single surface receives the interaction — the control itself, or a <label> that activates it. A label counts only if it is var(--target) square on its own; a control and its label are not added together across the gap between them. Controls nothing routes to (anything behind an open modal dialog) are not measured rather than being reported as 1x1. Anything matching touch-target-dense is measured against that contract's floor instead of this one's — it is a different floor, not an exemption from measurement.

touch-target-dense.summary: Deliberately compact controls follow shadcn/MUI-scale sizing rather than var(--target), and are measured against var(--target-min) (24x24, WCAG 2.2 AA SC 2.5.8) instead. This is a second floor, not an exemption: a dense control below 24x24 fails, under touch-target-dense. Three kinds qualify: dense inline affordances — a chip's remove glyph, a search field's clear button, rating stars, calendar day cells — a component's explicitly compact size variant, of which Button's size="sm" (36px) is the one the system ships, and a chip that is a control (<a class="ds-chip">, <button class="ds-chip">) at 32px. Reference for the painted scale: MUI Chip is 32px tall (24px small) with a 22px (16px small) delete icon; shadcn Badge is ~20px tall with 12px icons; shadcn Button sm is 36px. 36px clears WCAG 2.2 AA (SC 2.5.8, 24x24) with margin — var(--target) is AAA (SC 2.5.5) and this system's stricter default, not the standard. Choosing a compact variant is a design decision about density; it is not a licence to make a page's primary action small, and it is not a way to stop a control being measured — the 24x24 floor still applies and there is no marker below it.
touch-target-dense.check: The computed hit area of each compact control is at least var(--target-min) square, measured the same way touch-target-primary measures — on the control itself or on a <label> that activates it. The painted control stays at the shadcn/MUI reference scale; where the two differ, the hit area is expanded with padding or a bounded overlay rather than by inflating the paint, and that overlay must still satisfy hit-area-no-overlap. Compact controls are measured against this floor instead of touch-target-primary's, not exempted from measurement.
touch-target-dense.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/ai-patterns/testing/playwright → checkTouchTargets(), which measures anything matching data-touch-target="dense" or the system's own compact classes (DENSE_AFFORDANCE_SELECTOR, which includes .ds-button--sm and .ds-chip) against MINIMUM_TOUCH_TARGET_DENSE and reports a miss under this contract rather than touch-target-primary. The tier is keyed off the class, not off a React prop, so <a class="ds-button ds-button--sm"> is covered as well as <Button size="sm">, and <a class="ds-chip"> as well as <Chip>

hit-area-no-overlap.summary: An expanded hit area must never overlap sibling content. Bound the hit area — for example stretch it to the container's height, not a symmetric negative inset — so a control's overlay cannot cover an adjacent label.
hit-area-no-overlap.check: No interactive hit area intersects a sibling element's painted or interactive area.

ui-copy.summary: Functional UI copy — errors, empty states, helper and hint text, toasts, labels, button text, tooltips, confirmations, validation — is chrome. It states the fact, then the consequence, then the action, and stops. No unverifiable frequency claims ("almost always"), blame attribution ("on their side", "check your connection"), filler pacing ("in a moment", "hang tight"), unprompted reassurance or apology ("don't worry", "we'll sort it out"), escalation paths nobody asked for, or enthusiasm and exclamation marks. Reassurance is allowed only where it answers a question the reader is actually asking, and only as a fact: "You have not been charged." Past two short sentences, functional copy is explaining, reassuring or selling. This governs chrome only — a product's editorial voice in marketing prose, conversational surfaces and written deliverables is content, is a deliberate design decision, and is out of scope; where a surface mixes the two, the chrome follows this and the content is left alone.
ui-copy.check: No banned phrase appears in a copy prop (title, description, label, placeholder, helperText, error, tooltip, aria-label and friends) or in the children of a chrome component (Alert, Toast, Tooltip, Callout, Banner, EmptyState, FormMessage, …). Editorial content is out of scope and is not checked.
ui-copy.verifiedBy: @elirobinson/eslint-config → @elirobinson/no-padded-ui-copy, shipped as a warning so an upgrade cannot fail a consumer's build; raise it with designSystem({ copy: { severity: 'error' } }). The two-sentence limit and the content/chrome judgement are review, not lint.

tier-boundary.summary: Components live under packages/react/src/components/<tier>/. The tiers are not a fixed list — they are read off that directory layout into @elirobinson/react/manifest's `tiers`, which is the only roster; check it rather than assuming the set you last saw. Most tiers answer "how much is assembled here": a component that renders into a portal, traps focus, or manages open/closed state across multiple sub-elements is an organism; one assembled from 2+ atoms with no such orchestration is a molecule; otherwise an atom. `ai` is the exception and answers what the component is for. A component belongs in `ai/` when it has no meaning outside an assistant surface — a turn-taking message log, a token-by-token streaming affordance. The test is the domain, not the shape: if you can describe the component without saying "assistant", "model" or "streaming", it is not an `ai` component, whatever produced the content it renders. A card that happens to show a model's reply is still a Card. `ai/` inherits every other constraint here unchanged; being a tier buys a directory and nothing else.
tier-boundary.check: The component's directory is one of the tiers @elirobinson/react/manifest reports, and matches the boundary rule for its behavior — its domain for `ai`, how much it assembles otherwise.
tier-boundary.verifiedBy: not automated — review. @elirobinson/react/manifest names every tier that exists and the tier each component currently sits in; `ds list` groups the installed components by it.
